keyVerseText: And being not weak in faith, he considered not his own body now dead, when he was about an hundred years old, neither yet the deadness of Sarah's womb:
rootMeaning: The word ἑκατονταέτης (hekatontaétēs) derives from the Greek components ἑκατόν (hekatón), meaning 'hundred,' and ἔτος (étos), meaning 'year.' Thus, its root meaning literally denotes someone who is 'a hundred years old.' This etymology highlights the precise measurement of age, emphasizing a full century of life rather than a vague notion of advanced years. The literal sense enriches the English gloss 'hundred years old' by anchoring it firmly in the Greek numerical and temporal terms.
usageInScripture: This word appears only once in the New Testament, specifically in Romans 4:19, where it is translated as 'an hundred years old.' The singular occurrence reflects a consistent and specific use to describe the precise age of a person, emphasizing the exactness of the figure rather than a general approximation. Its use in the Septuagint (LXX) also aligns with this exactness in describing age, indicating a faithful translation from Hebrew expressions of age to Greek.
theologicalSignificance: The term ἑκατονταέτης carries profound theological significance by underscoring the reality of human mortality and the passage of time as established by God. In the biblical context, being one hundred years old is not just a milestone of longevity but a testament to God's sustaining power over life. The precision of the term reminds believers that God’s promises and faithfulness transcend human limitations, including age and physical condition. It invites faith in God’s ability to fulfill His promises despite natural obstacles, reinforcing the trustworthiness of divine power in the life of the believer.
keyVerseReflection: Romans 4:19 states, 'And being not weak in faith, he considered not his own body now dead, when he was about an hundred years old, neither yet the deadness of Sarah's womb.' The use of ἑκατονταέτης here highlights Abraham's advanced age as a tangible obstacle to God's promise of offspring. This precise age underscores the miraculous nature of God's promise being fulfilled, emphasizing that faith perseveres even when human circumstances seem impossible. The word enriches the verse by portraying Abraham's faith as unwavering despite the natural limitations implied by being a centenarian.
